title: Diogenes and Alexander the Great: 'Stand Out of My Sunlight!'
summary: In Corinth, when the conqueror Alexander the Great offered to grant any wish to the ascetic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope, Diogenes famously replied: 'Only stand a little out of my sun'.
keywords: Diogenes and Alexander the Great: 'Stand Out of My Sun!'
Diogenes of Sinope & Alexander the Great
full_text:
In the fourth century BCE, in the Greek city of Corinth, the philosopher Diogenes of Sinope lived a life of deliberate poverty. Rejecting social vanity, wealth, and conventional luxuries, he resided in a large discarded ceramic storage tub in the public square.

Following his victories across Greece, young King Alexander of Macedon visited Corinth. Statesmen, generals, and scholars thronged the royal court to pay homage, but Diogenes remained aloof.

Curious, Alexander took his retinue to the Craneion suburb to seek out the philosopher. He found Diogenes lying leisurely upon the grass, enjoying the morning warmth of the autumn sun.

Surrounded by guards clad in polished armor, Alexander stood over him and proclaimed with imperial magnificence:
"I am Alexander the Great. Ask of me whatever boon you desire, and by my sovereign power it shall be granted unto you!"

Diogenes shaded his eyes with one hand, looked up at the conqueror of nations, and replied with absolute composure:
"Only stand a little out of my sunlight. You are blocking the rays which you cannot give me, and which costs nothing to enjoy!"

Alexander’s officers laughed in scorn at what they considered crude impudence. But Alexander was stunned by the philosopher’s complete freedom from fear, ambition, and greed. Turning to his scoffing generals, the monarch uttered his legendary verdict:
"Truly I tell you, if I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes!"

Diogenes demonstrated that true sovereignty belongs not to those who conquer empires, but to those who have conquered their own desires.

moral: True contentment requires few possessions; he who masters his desires is richer and freer than the master of empires.
moral_reflection: True wealth is not the accumulation of possessions, but complete freedom from artificial desires.
witty_quote: True sovereignty belongs to him who desires nothing, for an emperor cannot gift the warmth of the sun that he himself blocks.
